title: Seeing and Unseeing the City: Photography, Power and Spatial Justice in Urban Co-Creation
content: Photography occupies a prominent and contested place in contemporary participatory urban planning. This research develops a critical-interpretative framework that rejects celebratory narratives of visual participation, whilst recognising the genuine possibilities that participatory photography can offer under appropriate political and institutional conditions. Drawing on recent literature, we examine four interrelated issues: i. access to participation and the exclusions it reproduces; ii. control over the production, selection, interpretation and circulation of images; iii. divergent spatial experiences and conflicts of use; iv. and the gap between representation and material change. The evidence gathered and analysed reveals tensions that methodological refinement alone cannot resolve, namely: researchers limit participants’ autonomy even in ostensibly co-produced projects; visual literacy and technological access remain unevenly distributed; images are selectively appropriated to legitimise predetermined institutional agendas; and emerging AI technologies risk intensifying these dynamics through algorithmic bias and a growing loss of trust in evidence. Participatory photography is understood here as a contested terrain, whose emancipatory potential depends on power relations, institutional conditions and the community’s control over the production and use of the images themselves.
